checks_performed: Read only the designated target input and draft; no web access or other source material was used.
Independently reconstructed the exact target-coverage judgment and audited all 18 claims by direct graph-theoretic arguments.
Created and ran <workspace-home>/paired_targeted_stress_v2_scratch/targeted_barbados_p31_geodesic_separator/audit-revision/bugbank/iter_1/exact_graph_checks.py using only integer graph operations.

The checker exhaustively tested all 2025 ordered pairs of geodesic vertex sets in K9, obstruction-family instances m=3 through 80, all 794 deletions of at most four vertices from I, and all 162 geodesic vertex sets in I.
The checker also verified an oriented 20-face sphere-embedding certificate for I, its diameter three, and the stated balanced two-geodesic witness. No floating-point decision was used.

claims.claim: It suffices to treat connected nonempty graphs.
claims.evidence: Let n>0. If every component already has at most n/2 vertices, choosing any two trivial geodesics and deleting their union cannot enlarge a component. Otherwise there is a unique component H with |H|>n/2. A solution inside H leaves H-pieces of order at most |H|/2<=n/2, while every other component has order at most n-|H|<n/2. Since H is a whole component, every path between its vertices remains in H, so its intrinsic distances and geodesics are unchanged in G.
claims.search_method: Independent case split on the component orders, including verification that distances are preserved inside a whole component.

claims.claim: Balancedness is monotone under enlarging the deleted set.
claims.evidence: For X subseteq Y, every component of G-Y is a connected subgraph of a single component of G-X. Its vertex count cannot be larger; with nonnegative weights, its weight cannot be larger either.
claims.search_method: Direct component-containment proof for both cardinalities and nonnegative weights.

claims.claim: In a connected graph, every set X of at most four vertices is contained in the union of two geodesics.
claims.evidence: For four vertices, partition X into two pairs and take a shortest path for each pair. For three vertices, use a shortest path through a chosen pair and a trivial path at the third vertex. Smaller cases follow by the same construction and padding with trivial paths. Connectivity guarantees that all required shortest paths exist.
claims.search_method: Exhaustive proof by the possible cardinalities 0 through 4.

claims.claim: Any graph having a half-balanced vertex separator of order at most four satisfies the two-geodesic conclusion; the same statement holds for arbitrary nonnegative vertex weights.
claims.evidence: In a connected graph, cover the separator by two geodesics using claim 2 and apply monotonicity. For a disconnected weighted graph of total weight W, if every original component has weight at most W/2, arbitrary geodesics suffice. Otherwise there is a unique heavy component H. The set X intersect H has at most four vertices, and deleting it leaves the same H-components as deleting X globally, each of weight at most W/2. Cover X intersect H by two H-geodesics; these are also G-geodesics. Other original components have total weight less than W/2. The unweighted case is the specialization to unit weights.
claims.search_method: Direct proof, with a separate heavy-component argument to check the disconnected and weighted quantifiers.

claims.claim: Every nonnegatively weighted finite tree has a centroid node whose deletion leaves tree components of weight at most half the total.
claims.evidence: For every edge, orient it toward an endpoint's side when that side has weight greater than W/2. At any node at most one incident far side can exceed W/2. Following outgoing edges cannot revisit a node and terminates because the tree is finite. At a terminal node no component of its deletion has weight greater than W/2.
claims.search_method: Direct heavy-side orientation proof, including the termination and terminal-node conditions.

claims.claim: Every vertex-weighted graph tree decomposition has a half-balanced bag.
claims.evidence: Assign each graph vertex and its weight to one bag containing it, and take a centroid t of the resulting weighted decomposition tree. If K is a component of G-B_t, each vertex's bag-subtree avoids t. Adjacent vertices have intersecting bag-subtrees, so connectivity of K places all those subtrees, and hence all assigned bags of vertices of K, in one component R of T-t. Nonnegative weights give w(K)<=w(R)<=W/2.
claims.search_method: Direct audit of the bag-subtree connectivity and weight-assignment argument.

claims.claim: If a connected graph has a tree decomposition in which every bag is contained in the union of two geodesics of the original graph, then those geodesics yield a half-balanced separator for every nonnegative vertex weighting.
claims.evidence: For the chosen weighting, claim 5 supplies a half-balanced bag B. By hypothesis B lies in the union Y of two original-graph geodesics. Since B subseteq Y, monotonicity shows that deleting Y remains half-balanced.
claims.search_method: Direct composition of the balanced-bag lemma with deletion monotonicity.

claims.claim: Every graph of treewidth at most three satisfies the target, even with arbitrary nonnegative vertex weights; planarity is unnecessary.
claims.evidence: A width-three decomposition has bags of at most four vertices. In a connected graph, claim 2 covers every bag by two original-graph geodesics, so claims 5 and 6 apply for every nonnegative weighting. For disconnected graphs, apply this to the unique component heavier than half the total weight, if one exists; otherwise the graph is already balanced. No step uses planarity.
claims.search_method: Direct deduction from the definition of treewidth, followed by an independent check of the disconnected weighted case.

claims.claim: In particular, every outerplanar graph and every planar graph with a universal vertex satisfies the target.
claims.evidence: An outerplane graph can be augmented, apart from trivial small cases, to a maximal outerplane graph. The triangular bounded faces and their weak-dual tree give a tree decomposition with three-vertex bags, proving treewidth at most two. If v is universal in a planar graph, deleting v leaves an embedding in which every remaining vertex is incident with the face formed around v, hence G-v is outerplanar. Adding v to every bag gives bags of size at most four, so claim 7 applies.
claims.search_method: Independent verification of the two required treewidth bounds via outerplane face bags and the universal-vertex deletion embedding.

claims.claim: If the largest component of an n-vertex graph has order m<=floor(n/2)+4, then the target holds. Consequently every nonempty graph on at most eight vertices satisfies it.
claims.evidence: Set q=floor(n/2). If m<=q, the graph is already balanced. Otherwise d=m-q lies in {1,2,3,4}. Deleting any d vertices from a largest component leaves every part of it with at most m-d=q vertices, while every other original component has at most n-m<=q vertices. This gives a balanced separator of order at most four, so claim 3 applies. For 1<=n<=8, m<=n<=floor(n/2)+4.
claims.search_method: Exact integer case analysis at the floor boundary, followed by the order-four separator theorem.

claims.claim: The preceding eight-vertex bound is sharp without planarity.
claims.evidence: In K9 every geodesic is either a singleton or one edge, so two geodesics delete at most four vertices. The complement is therefore a connected clique on at least five vertices, exceeding 9/2. The checker independently enumerated all 45 geodesic vertex sets and all 2025 ordered pairs and rejected every pair as a half-balanced separator.
claims.search_method: Analytic complete-graph argument plus exhaustive exact enumeration of all geodesic-set pairs in K9.
claims.witness: The complete graph K9 on vertices 0,1,...,8.

claims.claim: A connected graph satisfies the target whenever it has a half-balanced five-vertex separator X for which G[X] contains an induced path a-b-c.
claims.evidence: The edges ab and bc exist while ac does not, so a-b-c has length two and no length-one shortcut; it is a geodesic in G. A shortest path between the other two vertices of X exists by connectivity. The two geodesics cover X, and enlarging the deleted set preserves balance.
claims.search_method: Direct distance check for the induced three-vertex path and application of monotonicity.

claims.claim: A half-balanced isometric cycle is sufficient, regardless of its length.
claims.evidence: For a cycle of length k, partition its cyclic vertex order into two contiguous blocks of sizes floor(k/2) and ceil(k/2). Each block gives a cycle arc of length at most ceil(k/2)-1<=floor(k/2). Such an arc is a shortest path in the cycle, and isometry makes it a shortest path in G. The two arcs cover every cycle vertex, whose deletion is half-balanced by hypothesis.
claims.search_method: Direct parity-independent construction of two short cycle arcs.

claims.claim: In a planar graph, the vertex set of every half-balanced 5-cycle is coverable by two geodesics. A half-balanced induced cycle of length six is also coverable in any graph.
claims.evidence: For a 5-cycle, if all five pairs at cyclic distance two were adjacent, its five cycle edges and five chords would form a K5 subgraph, contradicting planarity. Hence some consecutive two-edge arc has nonadjacent endpoints and is geodesic; the two remaining cycle vertices are adjacent and form the second geodesic. For an induced 6-cycle, split the cyclic order into two consecutive triples. Each triple is a two-edge path whose endpoints are nonadjacent, hence a geodesic. In both cases the two paths cover the balanced cycle set.
claims.search_method: Complete chord analysis for C5 and direct induced-chord analysis for C6.

claims.claim: A balanced union of three specified geodesics need not have a balanced two-member subunion, even in a planar graph.
claims.evidence: The construction is planar because it is a 6-cycle with pendant leaves. It has n=3m+6 vertices. Deleting all three specified pendant edges leaves three components of order m. Deleting any two leaves components of orders 2m+2 and m, and 2(2m+2)>3m+6 exactly when m>2. Thus every m>=3 works. The checker verified these exact component counts for m=3 through 80 and also confirmed the alternative balanced pair described in the draft.
claims.search_method: Symbolic component counting for every m>=3, supplemented by parameterized exact graph checks.
claims.witness: Take m=3 in the cycle a-x-b-y-c-z-a, attach two leaves to each of a,b,c and one leaf xp,yp,zp to x,y,z, and specify the geodesics x-xp, y-yp, and z-zp. Their full union is balanced, while every two-member subunion leaves an 8-vertex component in a 15-vertex graph.

claims.claim: There is an explicit 12-vertex planar graph I of diameter three that remains connected after deletion of any four vertices.
claims.evidence: For the stated adjacency formula, the checker found 12 vertices, 30 edges, and degree five at every vertex. It verified 20 consistently oriented triangular faces: every undirected edge occurs twice with opposite orientations, every vertex link is one cycle, and V-E+F=2, giving a sphere embedding. Exact breadth-first searches give diameter three. All 794 vertex sets of cardinality zero through four were deleted, and the remaining graph was connected in every case.
claims.search_method: Exact combinatorial sphere-embedding certificate, all-pairs integer BFS, and exhaustive enumeration of all deletions through order four.
claims.witness: Vertices N,S,u0,...,u4,l0,...,l4 with edges N-ui, S-li, ui-u(i+1), li-l(i+1), ui-li, and ui-l(i-1), with indices modulo five.

claims.claim: The planar graph I has no half-balanced separator formed by one geodesic.
claims.evidence: Diameter three means every geodesic contains at most four vertices. Claim 15 then implies that deleting it leaves one connected component on at least 12-4=8 vertices, which exceeds the balance limit 6. Independently, the checker enumerated all 162 distinct geodesic vertex sets in I and found none balanced.
claims.search_method: Structural deduction from diameter and four-vertex connectivity, plus exhaustive geodesic enumeration.
claims.witness: The graph I specified in claim 15.

claims.claim: Two geodesics do half-balance I, so the preceding result establishes genuine necessity of the second path rather than a counterexample to the target.
claims.evidence: Both displayed paths have length three from u3 to l0. Those endpoints are nonadjacent and have disjoint neighborhoods, so their distance is at least three; the displayed paths show it is exactly three. Their union deletes N,u0,u1,u2,u3,l0. The six remaining vertices S,u4,l1,l2,l3,l4 form one connected component, exactly meeting the half-order bound. The checker verified both geodesics and this component calculation.
claims.search_method: Direct endpoint-distance certificate and exact deletion check.

target_evidence: The exact target is universal over all finite planar graphs. The draft proves material special cases, most notably all graphs of treewidth at most three, and several sufficient separator configurations. It does not establish that every planar graph falls into any of those cases. Its negative examples also do not disprove the target: K9 is nonplanar, the planar three-path family only obstructs discarding one of three specified paths and has another balanced geodesic pair, and I is explicitly balanced by two geodesics. Thus the universal planar question remains unresolved, while the surviving results constitute valid partial progress. The final writeup says exactly this, so claimed_resolution=PARTIAL is accurate rather than overstated or understated.
